title: The reflog is gone too. Find the commit with fsck.
summary: Last resort recovery: a commit nothing points at, in a repository whose reflog has been expired. Walk the object database directly and pull it back from nothing.
mental_model: Git never edits objects, only ever adds them. A commit becomes unreachable when no ref or reflog entry mentions it, but it stays in `.git/objects` until garbage collection actually prunes it. `fsck` walks that store and reports what nothing points at.

write.content:
def optimise(schedule):
    return sorted(schedule, key=lambda s: s['cost'])

commit.message: Filter expensive schedules in the optimiser

steps.title: Confirm how bad it is
steps.why: The branch was force-deleted and the reflog expired. Every normal recovery route is closed: `git log --all` shows nothing, and the reflog is empty.
steps.expect: One commit, no reflog entries, no experiment branch.

steps.title: Ask the object database directly
steps.why: `fsck --lost-found` walks every object in `.git/objects` and reports the ones no ref reaches. The commits are still there — nothing has pruned them yet.
steps.expect: dangling commit <sha> lines — your deleted work.

verify.label: unreachable commits are still in the object store

steps.title: Look at what you found
steps.why: A dangling sha is a normal commit; every read command works on it. Inspect before restoring — `fsck` will also list genuinely worthless objects from aborted operations.
commands: sh -c 'for sha in $(git fsck --lost-found 2>/dev/null | grep "dangling commit" | cut -d" " -f3); do echo "== $sha"; git log -1 --format="%h %s" $sha; done'
steps.expect: Both optimiser commits, identifiable by their messages.

steps.title: Restore the branch
steps.why: Point a branch at the newest dangling commit and the whole chain becomes reachable again — its parent comes back with it, because a commit references its history.

actions.run: sh -c 'git branch experiment/optimiser $(git log -1 --format=%H $(git fsck --lost-found 2>/dev/null | grep "dangling commit" | cut -d" " -f3 | head -20 | xargs -I{} git log -1 --format="%ct %H" {} | sort -rn | head -1 | cut -d" " -f2))'

steps.expect: The branch is back, with both commits.

verify.label: the branch is restored at the newest recovered commit

steps.title: Confirm the content really came back
steps.why: Not just the commit metadata — the trees and blobs were in the object store too. Check out the file and read it.

verify.label: the file content was recovered intact

steps.title: See what would have destroyed it
steps.why: `gc --prune=now` deletes unreachable objects immediately. Run it before recovery and there is genuinely nothing left — this is the one operation that makes git forget. Here the commits are reachable again, so gc leaves them alone.
steps.expect: The branch survives gc, because it is reachable now.

verify.label: the recovered branch survived garbage collection

steps.title: The habit that makes this unnecessary
steps.why: Before any destructive operation, drop a branch or tag on the tip. It costs one command and turns 'walk the object database' into 'switch branches'.

verify.label: both deleted commits were recovered from the object database
the file content came back with them
the branch is complete, including its parent commits

pitfalls: `git gc --prune=now` genuinely deletes unreachable objects. Do not run it while trying to recover something.
`fsck` also reports dangling blobs and trees from interrupted operations. Dangling commits are the interesting ones.
Automatic gc runs on its own when loose objects pile up, so 'the commits stay for 90 days' assumes the default `gc.pruneExpire`.
A repository cloned after the loss will not have the objects at all. Recovery must happen in the clone where the work was made.
cheatsheet: commits and blobs nothing points at

the command that actually deletes them — avoid mid-rescue
